en: The Commentary on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha, with Preface,
as Expounded by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai:
Regarding the Land of Bliss and the realm of suffering, the precious gold and jewels and the silt and sand, and the perspective of the womb-hell...

The lotus ponds and thorn forests compared to the jade trees truly arise from the distinction between defilement and purity within the mind, whereby one perceives the rising and sinking of the two lands;
as conduct unfolds as good or evil, one beholds the coarseness or subtlety of the two realms.

Just as a straight form produces a straight shadow and a turbid source results in murky flow, one knows that those who wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss must surely cultivate the sixteen sublime contemplations;
those who vow to see the World-Honored Amitābha must practice the three types of pure karma.

However, transformation proceeds through the gradual unfolding of events, and teaching arises in reliance upon conditions. Thus, when King Ajātaśatru committed patricide and Vaidehī offered her piteous plea, the Great Sage bestowed his compassion and expounded the Dharma according to the occasion. He manifested the radiant luster of his jade-like marks and displayed auspicious omens from his precious terrace; though he extensively revealed various sublime realms, the ultimate essence leads back to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), enabling those with karmic affinity in this degenerate age to follow this wondrous contemplation.
The setting sun hangs like a drum, marking the direction for the mind’s departure;
the great waters freeze into ice, truly manifesting the ground of lapis lazuli.
The wind whistles through jeweled leaves, flourishing in harmony with celestial music.
The golden channel of waves resonates in harmony with the sūtras;
one gazes upon the uṣṇīṣa while attending to the attendant, and contemplates the ūrṇā-kośa while beholding the Tathāgata.

When he closed his eyes and reached the end of his life, he leaped high up onto the precious terrace; as the inscription was completed and the seal dissolved, he was born through transformation seated upon a golden lotus.

It traverses the three grades of practitioners and cuts across them horizontally; it leaps over the five sufferings and gallops far ahead. It may truly be called the subtle practice, the wondrous contemplation, and the essential art of the ultimate Way.
This sutra takes the contemplation of the mind as its primary tenet and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence.

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha’s Teaching on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha": "Buddha" refers to the supreme object of visualization; by citing the primary retribution (the Buddha's own body), his supporting environment is included, and by describing the Master of Transformation, his retinue is encompassed.
Although there are sixteen contemplations, the mention of the Buddha encompasses them all; therefore, it is said that the Buddha taught the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.
As for "sūtra," it is glossed as "dharma" and "permanence."
Because it was spoken from the golden mouth of the Sage, it is called a *sūtra*.
There are five meanings for explaining a *sūtra*:
name (*nāman*), essence (*svabhāva*), tenet (*śarīra*), function (*kriyā*), and the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), and so forth.
First, regarding the explanation of the names: all sūtras possess both general and specific names. The general name is simply the character *jing* (sūtra). There are seven types of specific names:
they may consist of a single term for a person, a phenomenon (*dharma*), or a metaphor; or they may be compound, or complete.

Now, this sutra establishes its title based on the person who speaks it and the person spoken to; thus, while the teaching is distinct, it is collectively termed a "sutra. While the teaching is universal, the practices are not identical.
From the singular up to the immeasurable, the practices are distinct; yet in their common convergence upon eternal bliss, the practices are universal.

Although principle has no name, one uses the gates to name the principle; when the principle follows the gates, there are four times four, making sixteen, which constitutes the distinction between names and principles.
When the gates follow the principle, this constitutes the universal penetration of principle.
This explains the general and specific aspects by way of a single transformation.

Furthermore, by way of a single title: "The Buddha's teaching" refers to the doctrine (*śāsana*); "contemplation" refers to practice (*caryā*); and "Amitāyus Buddha" refers to the principle (*tattva*).
When teaching, practice, and principle are complete, there is naturally both a general and a specific meaning.

To explain this further by means of a single word, the *Śāstra* states: "Practice is as the teaching describes. Here, "describing" (*shuo*) refers to the teaching (*jiao*); "as" (*ru*) refers to the principle (*li*); and "practice" (*xing*) refers to the conduct (*xing*).
The Buddha is the Dharmakāya, contemplation is Prajñā, and Amitāyus is Vimukti.
One should know that these three are identical to one, and one is identical to the three; within the one, one understands the infinite, and within the infinite, one understands the one.
If even a single character can convey immeasurable meanings, how much more so must this be true for multiple characters, a title, a single sutra, or all the sutras!
Therefore, a sutra says: "If one hears even the name of the title, the merit obtained is beyond measure."
If one does not understand it as explained above, how could one obtain limitless merit? First, regarding the interpretation of "Buddha":

Buddha has the meaning of "awakening" (*buddha*), and there are six aspects of this. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings are themselves Buddhas; it is like the treasures and various goods fully present within the house of a poor woman, or the bright and perfect jewel on the forehead of a strongman."

The *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* cites ten parables: gold wrapped in tattered rags, an image within a clay mold, jars and basins in a dark room, and the seven treasures within a well; these have existed inherently from the beginning and are not merely present now.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings are suchness (*tathatā*).
The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* states: "The realm of the Buddha and the realm of sentient beings are one realm; there is no separate realm."
This is the Perfect Wisdom and Perfect Enlightenment of all phenomena, which pervades all places without anything being unclear.
Although there may be the five immediate transgressions, they are all the mark of liberation;
although there may be darkness, blindness, and delusion, their underlying principle remains present.

This principle is self-evident and eternally abiding in the world; it cannot be benefited by the presence of a Buddha, nor can it be diminished by the absence of a Buddha. To attain it does not constitute superiority, and to lose it does not constitute inferiority. Therefore, it is said that sentient beings are themselves Buddhas—this refers to the Buddha of Principle.
Regarding such a principle, were it not for the Buddha to teach it, no one would be able to know it.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "For one hundred and eighty kalpas, time passed in vain without a Buddha."
"When the World-Honored One has not yet appeared in the world, the ten directions are perpetually shrouded in darkness.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Throughout immeasurable eons, one has not even heard that a Tathāgata has appeared in the world, nor the names of Mahāyāna sūtras."

Only when a Buddha appears in the world can one fully manifest the sun of wisdom, recognize the radiance of the Triple Gem, open the gate of ambrosia, and know the wondrous flavor of the Ten Epithets.

Because this gave rise to understanding and brought joy regarding the Jewels, when Sudatta heard the name, the hairs on his body all stood on end; the pitch-black night became brilliantly clear, and the great gate opened of its own accord.
This is the Buddha of Name.

As for the Buddha of Contemplative Practice, one contemplates the Buddha’s marks and signs as if they were a cast golden image; the mind takes these wondrous forms as its object, confronting them with the eyes, so that whether the eyes are open or closed, in light or in darkness, one never departs from them.

He beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, from whom minor marks flowed forth from the ocean of great marks; vast and expansive like the waters at the end of a great kalpa, his gaze surveyed everywhere, and there was nothing that was not the Buddha-realm.

To contemplate one Buddha is to contemplate all Buddhas of the ten directions; to contemplate a present Buddha is to contemplate all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Their single body and single wisdom, as well as their powers and fearlessnesses, are likewise identical.

Meditating on the form-body, meditating on the Dharma-gates, and meditating on the true mark, one constantly maintains mindfulness such that there is no moment of non-mindfulness; every thought-moment is awakened.
This is called the Buddha of Contemplative Practice.
Regarding those who resemble the Buddha: by recollecting the body of the Buddha’s marks and signs, they attain a corresponding resemblance;
by recollecting the body of the Buddha’s Dharma-gates, they attain a corresponding resemblance;
by recollecting the body of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), they attain a corresponding resemblance.

"Similarity" refers to two things being analogous, such as brass resembling gold, or a melon compared to a gourd; it is like fire being first warm, or the sea being initially calm when one crosses it.
Water is extremely cold, but one knows it only upon drinking it.
If one does not dig a well when thirsty, what is the use of listening to the Dharma?
To briefly state its essentials: the "purity of the six sense faculties" as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is precisely its characteristic mark.
This is called the Buddha of Similarity.

As for the Buddha of Partial Realization, it refers to the first stage of the Abiding Mind (Prathamacittotpādavihāra): in a single arousal of the mind, all [aspirations] are aroused; one arouses all merits, arouses all wisdoms, and arouses all realms. These do not arise before or after one another, nor are they simultaneous; yet the three types of knowledge are attained within a single moment of mind.
Having attained the wondrous form-body of the Tathāgata, which serenely responds to all, one opens the secret treasury and abides therein by means of the dharma of non-abiding.

By universally manifesting the form-body to create various images, a single voice answers all sounds according to their kind; without moving from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the hearts of all beings are equally gladdened.

Those who should be saved by means of the three wheels can perfect the eight aspects of the Buddha’s path and manifest the majestic deportment of a Buddha; using the skillful means of the Buddha’s voice, they deliver and liberate them—how much more so those within the nine dharma-realms and their three wheels!
If this is already so for one at the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), how much more so for one at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)?
This is called the Buddha of partial realization (*vibhakta-sākṣāt-kriyā*).

As for the Ultimate Buddha, the Path has reached its consummation in the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathatā-gati*), reaching its ultimate limit; thus, only a Buddha can fully exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, with the wisdom of the limits perfected and the various enlightenments suddenly complete.
The Unsurpassed One (Anuttara) is named for having nothing further to be severed.
The Unsurpassed One is one beyond whom there is none superior.
He is like the moon on the fifteenth day, perfectly full and complete; he is the king among all the stars, most supreme, most excellent, and uniquely majestic in his splendor.
This is called the ultimate meaning of "Buddha.
Since the Buddha possesses immeasurable virtues, he should have immeasurable titles; yet, citing one encompasses all, for the *Avataṃsaka* contains one hundred thousand such titles.
Furthermore, there are ten thousand names for the sutras.

The Buddhas of the three periods of time universally possess the ten titles; even if one were to speak of the three titles in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* for the duration of an eon, one could not exhaust them, let alone all the other titles.

To "expound" means to take pleasure in what one harbors within; that is, the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the eighty thousand dharma-treasuries, and all dharma-gates such as the six perfections and the four immeasurables.

Furthermore, within a single dharma, one makes distinctions through four gates, skillfully applying the benefits of the four *siddhāntas* within each gate. Those who hear this rejoice, praise its utility, and accept it for practice; their faith, precepts, diligence, and mindfulness are thereby awakened, while greed, anger, and delusion suddenly melt away like ice. Thus, they transform from the state of an ordinary person into a sage and enter the flowing stream of the Dharma.
There may be three, two, or one benefit; if there is no benefit at all, then it is better to remain silent.
If a single capacity is struck and the Sage bestows the four benefits through one gate, the same applies to the other three gates.
Just as it is when one condition is explained by means of one dharma, so it is for all conditions and all dharmas.
As for "contemplation" (*guan*), there are three successive contemplations. Within a single mind, there are these three contemplations:

the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional is also called the contemplation of the two truths; the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness is also called the contemplation of equality; and the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way is attained through the two emptinesses as a skillful means. With each thought-moment becoming quiescent, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
This name is derived from the *Sutra of the Garland* (*Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*).
To explain its meaning now: "provisional" refers to that which is false and illusory, which is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
"emptiness" refers to that which is examined and real, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Now, desiring to leave the mundane world and return to the Truth, one speaks of the contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional.

The provisional is the means by which one enters emptiness; first, one must contemplate the provisional, and by knowing the provisional to be illusory and false, one attains union with the True. Therefore, this is called the contemplation of the two truths.
If this contemplation is perfected, one immediately realizes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
As for those who enter the contemplation of the provisional from emptiness (*śūnyatā*): if they were to abide in emptiness, how would they differ from the followers of the Two Vehicles?
One would fail to accomplish the Buddha-dharma and fail to benefit sentient beings.

Therefore, one contemplates emptiness and, without dwelling in emptiness, enters into the provisional; knowing the illness and identifying the medicine, one administers the medicine according to the illness so that it may be taken and practiced. This is called the contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness.
As for what is called "equality," it is termed equality in relation to what preceded it.

Previously, one used emptiness to break through the provisional; now, one uses the provisional to break through emptiness. Since the application of these two modes of negation is equal, it is called the contemplation of equality.
When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the Knowledge of the Modes of Phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).

Regarding "the two emptinesses as the means": first one contemplates the emptiness of saṃsāra, and next one contemplates the emptiness of nirvāṇa; these two emptinesses serve as the means for simultaneous negation (*ubhayanirodha*).
First one contemplates the function of emptiness, and next one contemplates the function of the provisional; these two functions serve as the skillful means for simultaneous illumination.
With every thought returning to and entering the ocean of *sarvajñā*, one simultaneously illuminates the two truths.
When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
This constitutes the third contemplation in sequence.
As for "the three contemplations in a single mind," this is derived from the *Śāstra* (*Vyākhyā*).
The Treatise states: "The three wisdoms are substantially one within a single mind.

To attain this is to have three contemplations through a single contemplation, and to contemplate the three truths through a single truth; therefore, it is called the "three contemplations in a single mind" (ekacitta-trisamādhi).
It is analogous to how a single mind possesses arising, abiding, and ceasing; thus these three marks exist within a single mind.
When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the three wisdoms within a single mind, which is also termed the "wisdom of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā).
One knows all the various types of characteristics and appearances of the state of quiescent extinction (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*).
That which is the state of quiescent extinction is the power of the simultaneous negation of both [subject and object].
That one knows all the various appearances is the power of the simultaneous illumination of both.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are themselves emptiness, themselves the provisional, and themselves the Middle. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The three types of wisdom are actually attained within a single moment of mind. This is precisely that meaning.

This contemplation is subtle and wondrous: it is three within one, and one within three; one contemplation is all contemplations, and all contemplations are one contemplation. It is neither one nor many—such is the contemplation that encompasses all contemplations.

Regarding "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus), in India it is called Amitābha Buddha. Fundamentally, he has no body, no life, and no measure; yet, in accordance with worldly conventions, we speak of his three bodies, and in accordance with worldly conventions, we speak of his three lifespans, and in accordance with worldly conventions, we speak of his three measures.
As for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), it takes the nature of reality (dharmatā) as its model and, in turn, takes that very nature of reality as its body.

This body is neither material substance nor mental consciousness; it is not comprised within the aggregates, elements, or sense bases. It is merely a provisional designation of the nature of reality as the "Dharma-body."

Regarding the "life-span of the dharma-nature," it is not a life-faculty obtained through karmic retribution, nor does it possess continuity; rather, it is merely designated as "life" because it is neither shifting nor changing.
This life has no measure of length, nor any measure of brevity; it neither extends nor shortens, and is merely designated as being equal in measure to the dharma-realm and empty space.
This is precisely the body that is no-body, the life-span that is no-life-span, and the measurement that is no-measurement.
As for the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), it is what is elicited through spiritual cultivation.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states, "That which is obtained through long-cultivated practice," and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states, "Because Great Parinirvāṇa is attained through the path of cultivation. Thus, the wisdom of suchness illuminates the realm of suchness; bodhi-wisdom and the dharma-nature are in mutual resonance and profound union.
"Correspondence" is like the fit between a box and its lid.
"Mutual merging" is like water and milk merging together.

The Dharma-body is neither body nor non-body; since wisdom both corresponds and merges with it, it is likewise neither body nor non-body, yet this wisdom is conventionally designated as the Reward-body (Sambhogakāya).
The Dharma-life is neither life nor non-life; since wisdom corresponds to the profound mystery, it is likewise neither life nor non-life, yet we forcibly name this "non-life" as "life.

The Dharma-measure is neither measure nor immeasurability; since wisdom corresponds to the profound mystery, it is likewise neither measure nor immeasurability, yet we forcibly name this "immeasurability" as "measure."

As for the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), it corresponds to all things by taking them as its body; it corresponds to their continuity by taking it as its lifespan; and it corresponds to their dimensions by taking them as its measure.
Wisdom is merged with the essence, enabling the arousal of great function, just as mercury mixed with pure gold can coat various forms and images.
The merit and the Dharma-body manifest and appear everywhere; they can manifest as a body or as a non-body, as eternal life or as impermanent life, and as the immeasurable or as the measurable.
There are two meanings of "measurable" (*pramāṇa*):
first, it is the measure of the immeasurable; second, it is the measure of the measurable.
For example, [the figures of] seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and eighty [kalpas], and so forth, are measures of the measurable.
If Amitābha truly had a fixed limit, then humans and devas would be unable to count it; this is the "immeasurable within the measurable.
All response-buddhas (nirmāṇakāyas) possess both types of measure, varying in length and brevity according to phenomena and conditions.
However, these three bodies and their three lifespans cannot be regarded as either identical or distinct; to do so would contradict the nature of the Dharma.
Only by being three while being one, and one while being three, does one truly accord with the profound text.
The explanation of the names is concluded.
Next, we shall examine the essence (*tattva*). Essence refers to the primary substance.
As the *Śāstra* states: "With the exception of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), everything else is the work of Māra."

The Mahāyāna sūtras take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their seal and as the essential body of the sūtra; they are adorned by immeasurable merits, all various practices converge toward it, and it is elucidated through discourse and dialogue. It is like the myriad stars encircling the North Star, or like the ten thousand streams flowing into the Eastern Sea; therefore, the true mark is taken as the essence of the sūtra.
When calligraphers interpret the *Book of Rites*, they explain it in terms of "form" (*ti*).
Form comprises distinctions of honor and humility, as well as seniority and juniority; the form of a sovereign or father is honorable, while the form of a minister or son is humble.
One should understand that this interpretation of the ritual form is the method for attaining the ultimate nobility.

Furthermore, "essence" (*tī*) means "bottom. To exhaust the source and reach the bottom, to fully fathom the depths of principle, and to thoroughly penetrate the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), is what is called the "bottom.
The *Śāstra* states: "In the great ocean of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), only the Buddha reaches its bottom. Thus, the term "bottom" is used to explain "essence."

Furthermore, "essence" (tǐ) carries the meaning of "penetration. When one attains this essence, the mind penetrates all things without obstruction, like the wind moving through space with sovereign freedom and no hindrance; thus, all various names and distinct explanations do not contradict the true nature of reality (dharmatā).

The *Śāstra* states: "Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha has spoken of it by various names. Therefore, the essence of the sūtra is explained through the realization of its fundamental nature (*tattva*).
Next, the core tenet (*śarīra*) of the sūtra is elucidated.
First, the essence of the school is briefly distinguished; second, the school itself is formally elucidated. Some say:
the school is identical to the essence, and the essence is identical to the school.
What is currently not employed? Why?
Because while the schools are two, their essence is non-dual.
If the substance were dual, then substance would not be substance;
if the thesis were non-dual, then the thesis would not be a thesis.

Just as beams and pillars are the structural supports of a house, while the void of the house is that which is occupied by the beams and pillars, one should not say that the beams and pillars are the void of the house, nor that the void of the house is the beams and pillars.
If the thesis and the essence were one, the fault would be as described above.

If the thesis and the essence were different, then the two things would exist in isolation: the thesis would not be a thesis that reveals the essence, and the essence would not be the essence belonging to the thesis.
The "tenet" (zong) is not a tenet that reveals the essence; if it were a tenet, it would be erroneous and inverted, lacking the seal of truth.

The "essence" (ti) is not an essence belonging to a school of tenets; if it were such an essence, it would be narrow and incomplete, implying that various phenomena exist apart from the nature of reality (dharmatā).
If the essence of the thesis were different [from its attributes], the fault would be as described above.
Now, it is said that they are not different yet are different; therefore, there is a thesis that is both manifold and one, and thus there is an essence.
The central tenet of this sutra is that if the mind is purified through contemplation, then the Buddha-land is purified; this constitutes the primary purpose of the scripture.

There are four kinds of pure lands: the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages, the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder, the Land of True Reward Without Obstruction, and the Land of Eternal Quiescence and Radiance. Each of these possesses both pure and impure aspects.
The gravity of the five turbidities constitutes the distinction between the pure and the impure in their cohabitation.
The analysis of essence versus function constitutes the distinction between the pure and the impure in the state of having a remainder.
Gradual entry versus sudden entry constitutes the distinction between the pure and the impure in the stage of true retribution.
Partially realizing the ultimate, one perceives the quiescent light as pure or impure.
The Sahā world, with its mixture of evil, brambles, rubble, and pervasive impurity, is the defiled realm of cohabitation.

The Land of Peaceful Nurturing is pure; its ponds flow with water of eight virtues and its trees are arrayed with the seven treasures. It is next to *nirvāṇa*, where all belong to the assembly of those fixed in right determination, and ordinary beings and sages dwell together; it is the superior grade of pure land.
Regarding "the path of skillful means with remainder": one cultivates the path of skillful means to sever the delusions of the four abodes; hence it is called "skillful means.
Because ignorance has not yet been exhausted, it is said to be "with remainder."

The *Śāstra* states: "Beyond the triple world there is a Pure Land, wherein Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born; they receive a Dharma-nature body rather than being born through the process of segmented birth."

The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are those who have truly attained arhatship yet do not believe in this Dharma, they shall, upon encountering another Buddha, attain definitive understanding within this Dharma."
Within this, there are further distinctions of sharp and dull faculties: that which points upward is considered pure, while that which points downward is considered defiled.

Regarding "the true retribution of non-obstruction": by practicing the Dharma of reality, one realizes a superior retribution in which the physical and mental aggregates do not obstruct one another; therefore, it is called "non-obstruction."
It is an abode for pure bodhisattvas alone, with no followers of the two vehicles.
As the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "The three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages abide in the fruition of retribution"—this is precisely its meaning.
The *Śāstra* states: "The supreme and wondrous five desires of the Bodhisattvas can cause Kāśyapa to rise and dance.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of "immeasurable clouds of incense terraces," which refers precisely to the pure and wondrous five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of that land.
Within this, one further discusses the sequence, sudden awakening, the superior and inferior, the pure and the defiled, and so forth.

As for the "Eternally Quiescent Light" (*nitya-prabhāsvara*): "eternal" is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), "quiescent" is liberation (*vimukti*), and "light" is wisdom (*prajñā*). These three points are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither combined nor separate; they are called the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*).
The dwelling places where the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, roam and reside are truly eternal, ultimate, and supremely pure lands.
They differ only in terms of being partially attained or ultimately perfected, superior or inferior, and pure or impure.
Therefore, the core tenet of this sutra is that the sublime contemplation of mind-cultivation can bring about rebirth in a Pure Land.
Next, we shall examine the function of the sutra.
"Function" refers to its efficacious power; the generation of goodness and the eradication of evil constitute the sutra's power and function.
It is called "power" (*bala*) because it extinguishes evil; it is called "function" (*kāritra*) because it gives rise to goodness.
It is called "merit" (*guṇa*) because it extinguishes evil; it is called "virtue" (*guṇa*) because it gives rise to goodness.
These are all partial designations; a complete discussion must necessarily include them all.
Suffering is the evil fruit, while greed, anger, and delusion are the evil causes.
If the evil causes are not eliminated, the fruit cannot be extinguished.
Therefore, this sutra can cause even the five heinous crimes to be extinguished and lead one to rebirth in the Pure Land; this is precisely the great power and function of this sutra.
Regarding its doctrinal classification, this is subsumed within the Mahāyāna Vaipulya teachings.
Adapting to the capacities of beings and employing various means of conversion, it appears in both extensive and abbreviated forms;

the original version in two fascicles was translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, while this present version was translated by Jñānayaśas in Yangzhou during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
Both sutras were preached in Rājagṛha.
Furthermore, there is a shorter version titled the *Amitābha-sūtra*, which was preached in Śrāvastī.
*Amitābha* and *Amitāyus* are regional dialects for the same name.
Regarding the meaning clarified by the two Piṭakas, this is subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
As for the gradual and sudden modes of awakening and entry, this constitutes the Sudden Teaching.

Since it was specifically for Vaidehī and her attendants—all of whom were ordinary beings who had not yet realized the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle—it is known to be sudden, rather than entering through the gradual path.

The title designates this as "Spoken by the Buddha" (*buddhabhāṣita*) to distinguish it from the discourses spoken by the four types of persons: disciples, various sages (*ṛṣi*), devas, and emanated beings (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*).
The text is divided into three sections:
the introduction (*nidāna*), the main body (*śarīra*), and the dissemination (*parīndanā*).
From "Thus" up to "the pure object of meditation" constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*).

"At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha as to what [this sutra] should be named," from here until the end of the scripture, constitutes the *parīndanā* (circulation) section.
Within the introduction (*nidāna*), there are two parts:
the testimony of faith (*śraddhā-prasāda*) and the incitement (*utthāna*).
The correct exposition also has two parts:
pure karma and sublime contemplation.
The circulation [of the teaching] likewise has two parts:
The Royal Palace and Vulture Peak. The initial *nidāna* (序) consists of six phrases: "Thus" (*evam*) indicates faith;

"I have heard" (*śrutam mayā*) distinguishes [the teaching] from that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) clarifies the cessation of dispute; "Buddha" (*buddha*) correctly identifies the principal teacher; "Royal City" (*rājadhānī*) discusses the place of residence; and the listing of the assembly constitutes those who heard it together.
“Thus” (*evam*) means that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena remains unchanged throughout past and present; this is termed “thusness” (*tathatā*).
Because it is spoken in accordance with suchness, it is called “is” (*iti*).
Because it is definitively trustworthy, it is said to be “thus” (*evam*).
The phrase "I have heard" distinguishes [this teaching] from that of the non-Buddhists, indicating that there was a direct transmission.
"I" (aham) carries the sense of sovereignty.
Since all phenomena are empty and devoid of self, why is "I" spoken of?
Following worldly convention, one speaks of a "self" as a provisional designation; that is to say, it is a name for views and conceit.
If there were no self, there would be no hearing [the Dharma];
if there were no hearing, the transformative teaching would be severed.

For this reason, although one knows there is no self, for the sake of ensuring the continuity of the transmission and transformation [of the Dharma], one speaks of a "self" by way of conventional designation.
It is like a person exchanging gold coins for copper coins, wood, grass, and so forth; such is the nature of buying and selling, and no one laughs at it.
Therefore, it is said, "I have heard.
As for the term "one," the Buddha-dharma has no fixed or substantial oneness; why then is it called "one"?
It is merely designated as "one" as a conventional, provisional expression.
The *Śāstra* extensively refutes the views of identity and difference.
Regarding "time," there are two kinds:
first, *kāla*, which refers to a short duration and is also termed "real time."
Second, *samaya* is called "long time" and is also called "conventional time.
Here, regardless of whether it is long or short, real or conventional, once this sutra has been finished being preached, it is collectively termed "at one time."
"Buddha" is also *bhagavat*, which here means "possessing great fame and renown," and is also said to mean "one who can destroy afflictions.
A Buddha is so named because of their impartial awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Thus, they are called a Buddha.

Being able to awaken oneself and further able to awaken others, with both awakening and practice fully perfected—his omniscience distinguishes him from non-Buddhists, his compassion distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles, and his equanimity distinguishes him from lesser bodhisattvas; this state of supreme honor is called Buddhahood.

Regarding "being present" (*zai*): to be for a brief moment is called being present, while to remain for a long duration is termed abiding (*zhu*). This is merely a general way of speaking. As for "abiding":

all four modes of deportment constitute abiding; their specific distinctions are the Celestial Abode (*deva-vihāra*), the Brahma Abode (*brahma-vihāra*), the Noble Abode (*ārya-vihāra*), and the Buddha Abode (*buddha-vihāra*).
The celestial abodes refer to the six heavens of the desire realm; their causes are generosity, ethical discipline, and a virtuous mind.
The Brahma abodes range from the first dhyāna to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; their causes are the four immeasurable minds.
The "Noble Abodes" refer to the three vehicles; their causes are the three samādhis.
The "Buddha Abode" refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the hundred-and-eight samādhis, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Regarding "Rājagṛha," in India it is called Rājagṛha-kāra. The *Śāstra* (Treatise) explains:
A queen of the King of Magadha gave birth to a son who had one head, two faces, and four arms; people deemed him an ill omen.
The king immediately tore apart his body and head and cast them into the wilderness.
A rākṣasī named Śālā returned, rejoining his body and nourishing him with her milk.
Later, when he grew to adulthood, his strength enabled him to unify the various states and rule over the world.

He took eighteen thousand kings from various kingdoms and established them upon these five mountains; ruling Jambudvīpa with great power and majesty, the people of Jambudvīpa therefore named this city Rājagṛha (the City of the King’s Abode).
Furthermore, in the city where they had previously resided, a fire broke out; one house was burned down and another rebuilt, and this occurred as many as seven times.
The people were exhausted by the labor, so they assembled various wise men and decided it was appropriate to move to another location.

He immediately searched for a site and saw these five mountains surrounding one another like a city wall; he then constructed a palace and resided within it, which is why it is called Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence).

Furthermore, in ancient times there was a king named Vasu who grew weary of the world and studied the ways of the immortals; he falsely claimed that living beings must be slaughtered and their flesh consumed during celestial sacrifices, and consequently fell into hell.
His son, Guangche (Broad Vehicle), succeeded him as king.
He reflected to himself:
"My father entered hell while still alive; now, if I wish to leave the household life, I fear falling into hell, yet if I wish to govern the world, I fear committing transgressions."
"Where shall my body be?
As he was thinking this, a voice spoke from the air: "Go!"
"If one sees a place that is difficult to encounter and rare, one should establish a dwelling there.

While the king was out hunting, he saw a deer running as swiftly as the wind; the king pursued it to this mountain, which was surrounded by steep and solid crags. Its ground was level and even, with fine, soft grass growing there and beautiful flowers covering the earth. The lush forests were filled with blossoms and fruit, and the hot springs and bathing pools were all pure and pristine.
The heavens rained down celestial incense and played celestial music.
As soon as the gandharvas and others saw the king arrive, they each departed.
Because he built a palace within this place of such spiritual wonders, it was named Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence).
"Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata" (Vulture Peak) is translated as "Numinous Vulture" (Língjìu), for it is there that various sages, seers, and spirits dwell.
It is also called "Vulture Head" (Jiùtóu), as the shape of its peaks resembles a vulture.
Furthermore, to the south of the mountain is a śītavana (cemetery). After various vultures have finished feeding on corpses, they roost upon that mountain.

However, the Dharma-body is formless and in reality does not depend on a specific location for its dwelling; it is only for the sake of benefiting others that the transformation body manifests according to circumstances, clarifying the abode where the master of transformation resides.
The passage beginning with "Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus" lists the audience who heard the teaching.
First the śrāvakas, then the bodhisattvas; this demonstrates that, within the teaching, the external manifestations of the two vehicles are presented as superior.

Why are their virtues not extolled?
It is not that they lack virtue; rather, it is because the translators of the scriptures were brief.

"With" (yǔ) has the meaning of "together. Because they share one place, one time, one mind, one precept, one path, one view, one liberation, and so forth—all being one—it is therefore called "together."

As for the term "bhikṣu," there are six meanings regarding cause and effect:

as causes, they are named "mendicant" (bhikṣu), "terrorizer of Māra," and "destroyer of evil"; as effects, they are titled "worthy of offerings" (arhat), "slayer of thieves," and "one who does not arise again" (anupapatti).
The *Śāstra* records that Viśuddhacakṣus asked Śāriputra:

Cultivating fields and planting medicinal herbs is called 'downward-facing food' (*adhomukha-bhakṣa*). Looking upward at the stars and constellations is called 'upward-facing food' (*ūrdhvamukha-bhakṣa*). Employing clever speech in the four directions is called 'four-directional food' (*caturmukha-bhakṣa*). Using incantations, arts, divination, and calculation is called 'four-intermediate-directional food' (*vidig-mukha-bhakṣa*)."
A bhikṣu who does not perform these four things is called a pure mendicant.

As for "terrifying Māra": when one resolves to leave the household life, the yakṣas who roam the earth proclaim it; those who fly through the air pass the news on in succession until it reaches the six heavens of the desire realm.
Upon hearing this, the Māra King was terrified that his followers would be lost.
As for "Destroyer of Evil," it means one who can destroy afflictions; because all ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are completely shattered and severed, he is named the Destroyer of Evil.

"Community" (saṃgha) refers to a group of four or more, up to hundreds, thousands, or even immeasurable numbers, who perform the formal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) and the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*) for the *poṣadha* in a single location; when both the matter and the principle are in harmony and there is no conflict or dispute, it is called a "harmonious community."
First, there are monks with a sense of shame who maintain the precepts without transgression.

Of these two groups, while they may perform formal acts (karmavācanā) together and share in the same hearing and realization of faith, here only those beyond training are taken.

Seeing that Prince Ajātaśatru possessed the marks of a great king, he transformed his own body into an elephant or a horse-treasure and embraced and kissed the prince before him. Furthermore, he went up to heaven to fetch celestial flowers and celestial food, saying to the prince:
“I shall become a new Buddha, and you shall become a new king;
will this not be joyful!
Thus, following an evil friend, he seized his father, the King.

The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā rebuked him; she struck him with her fist until his eye was dislodged.
Having committed three heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), he entered hell alive.
In the past, when Bimbisāra was wandering on Mount Vipula to hunt deer, he returned empty-handed with no catch.
He encountered a seer sitting upright; he had his men drive him away and subsequently ordered him to be killed.
At the moment of death, he harbored an evil thought:
"In my future life, may I likewise harm you with mind and mouth, just as you have done today."
Such matters as these are all the skillful means (*upāya*) manifested by the Great Being, who practices non-ways to penetrate the Buddha-way.

Because the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ, their entry into the Way varies; whether through one transgression or one compliance, he propagates the Way and benefits all things. He manifests the practice of uninterrupted [karma] yet remains free from affliction or anger; King Ajātaśatru manifests transgression to cause those who do evil to cease their rebellious intent.

The text is divided into two parts:
first, the identification of the petitioner; second, the content of the request.

Maudgalyāyana was her teacher and preceptor, while Ānanda was the Buddha’s attendant; because they had constantly provided her with instruction and admonition in the past, she specifically sought to see them.
Dwelling within the secluded palace, she did not dare to seek [the Buddha] privately; weary of the realm of internal defilements, she aspired to be born in the Pure Land.

Desiring to have two people convey her intent and invite the Buddha, she wept with tears falling like rain, looking toward the Buddha with the hope that he would look upon her with compassion, and prostrated herself from afar in worship.
